zones.label: Column 1
zones.note: Lexical aid consulted after the independent scan reading: Entry Words Data of Nippojisho, NINJAL, Hideyuki Ohshima and Taichi Aida, version 202510; supplied page subset, CC BY 4.0. https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/ This aid supports lexical identification, not this copy's glyphs, spacing, or typeface.

lines.note: Nadaracani is the adverb corresponding to Nadaracana at the end of f345. The r is visible, correcting OCR t; the brief Aduer. label does not supply a new definition.

runs.text: Nadare, uru, eta. l, nadare vochi, ru.

lines.note: Nadare and the alternative nadare vochi describe sliding or coming down from above. The printed l introduces the alternative rather than belonging to either Japanese verb.

runs.text: correndo, ou eſcorregando de lugar alto pe-

lines.note: The Portuguese describes running or slipping from a high place. Pe- belongs to pera on the next row and is retained as a visible physical division.
Completes the downward direction and illustrates wax running down. Rǒ is wax; its clearly printed caron is preserved instead of imposing the expected modern long-vowel spelling.

runs.text: a cera de cima pera baixo derretida. ¶

lines.note: The melted wax flows from top to bottom. A second example begins with Su-, which joins miga below to refer to charcoal or embers.
Completes Sumi ga nadaruru. The Portuguese identifies this as terminology used in tea practice, with the setting and explanation supplied on the following rows.

runs.text: Chano yǔ. Ideſt, abaixarẽ ſe as braſas, & des-

lines.note: Chano yǔ names the tea setting; the embers settle down and disintegrate into ash. The visible mark over u is a caron, not the OCR tilde. The full embedded Japanese phrase is included for typeface review.
Completes desfazerem se em cinza, crumbling into ash. This explains the behaviour of the embers in the preceding technical expression.
Nade, with the printed nazzuru principal form, means gently passing the hand over something. The double z and the historical inflection are not modernized to naderu.

Completes the physical stroking sense and introduces a metaphorical use. The upright Per met. apparatus is distinguished from the surrounding italic gloss after the second comparison. Ta- is the beginning of tami, the people, continued with its object particle below.
Tami wo nazzuru means treating the people compassionately. The translation first mentions cultivators, with lauradores divided at the physical line end.

runs.text: res, ou pouo fazendo lhe fauor. ¶

lines.note: Completes the benevolent treatment of cultivators or the people. The next example begins Come, rice, and continues with the object-marked verb on the following row.
Come wo nazzuru means pounding rice. The narrow but visible word gap in Pilar arroz is restored; Nadez- begins the name of the pounding implement below.
Completes Nadezzuchi, a mallet for pounding rice. The two z letters are distributed across the physical line division and must not be collapsed into one.
Nadeague combines passing the hand over something with lifting it upward. The first explanation concerns raising the hair by stroking over the head.

runs.text: da cabeça aleuãtar os cabelos, ou por cima dou

lines.note: The hand lifts the hair on the head or passes over another object. The nasal abbreviation in aleuãtar and the unhyphenated division dou / tra are preserved.
Tra completes doutra. The example introduces two young people; its continuation describes placing them on the speaker's two knees and smoothing their hair upward.

runs.text: uo ſayǔno fizani voite, vocureno camiuo

lines.note: The two young people are placed on the left and right knees, followed by the object phrase concerning their loose or trailing hair. The historical spelling vocureno is retained.
Nadeague completes the hair-stroking action. Qir. is an upright citation label, retained without expanding its source name; the Portuguese translation begins the divided word moços.

runs.text: ços ſobre os joelhos direito, & eſquerdo, &

lines.note: The two young people sit on the right and left knees. This translation corroborates the Japanese sayǔ and the bodily arrangement in the preceding example.

runs.text: pondo lhe a mão ſobre as cabeças lhes aleuanta-

lines.note: The speaker places a hand over their heads and raises their hair. The imperfect verb is visibly divided after aleuanta- and finishes on the next row.
Completes the gentle raising of the hair. A second example starts Tçuchi wo, introducing earth or clay as the object instead of hair.

runs.text: Aleuantar o barro com as mãos

lines.note: Tçuchi wo nadeaguru means pushing clay upward with the hands. The printed -aguru form is retained rather than normalized to a modern conjugation.

runs.text: pera cima quando vai caindo pera baixo, como

lines.note: The clay is pushed upward as it tends to fall down. The following row provides wall plastering as the concrete example of this action.
Wall plastering illustrates pushing clay upward while it tends to slip down. The historical verb barrão is retained without modern spelling changes.
Nadeguine is another name for a rice-pounding mallet. Its guine component and the identical gloss connect it with the Nadezzuchi implement already mentioned.
Nadetçuqe means rubbing or smoothing something down with the hand. The partly worn initial of Esfregar is retained from the readable word and surrounding definition.

runs.text: pegando, ou aßentando a couſa. Vt,

lines.note: The rubbing fixes or settles the object in place. The example begins Cami, which the following Portuguese translation identifies as paper rather than the homophonous hair.
Cami wo nadetçuquru means pressing or smoothing paper into place. The mixed long-and-short s sequence in aſsentar is retained instead of regularized to another double-s form.
The object is explicitly paper, smoothed by hand. A second example applies the verb to a person, preparing the figurative sense explained below.

runs.text: Grangear, & trazer à ſua parte com mimos

lines.note: Fito wo nadetçuquru is explained as winning someone over with favours or affectionate treatment. The historical Grangear is preserved rather than modernized.
Completes the figurative construction with someone as its object. This short line closes the explanation of winning a person over.

runs.text: Modo de amarrar os cabelos da

lines.note: The entry describes tying the hair back. Although the following example uses nadetçuqe, this headword visibly has gue, including a descending g; the printed Naguetçuqe anomaly is retained rather than silently emended.

runs.text: cabeça botados pera de tras. Vt,

lines.note: The hair is gathered toward the back of the head. Cami wo na- begins the example with hair as the object, contrasting with the paper sense above.
Completes nadetçuqeni yǔ, tying the hair in this arrangement. Its de spelling differs from the entry's printed gue; both local forms are preserved and the discrepancy is documented.

runs.text: maneira. ¶ Item, O meſmo homem que

lines.note: Completes tying the hair in this way, then extends the noun to the person who wears the hairstyle. The relative clause continues on the next row.

runs.text: traz deſta maneira os cabelos amarrados.

lines.note: The added sense is the man whose hair is tied in this fashion. This metonymic use is explicitly part of the same entry.

runs.text: Erua que dà hũa flor como crauos.

lines.note: Nadexico corresponds to nadeshiko, described as a plant with a flower resembling carnations. The visible i after x is restored; no more precise botanical identification is imposed.
Nadezzuchi is separately entered as a rice-pounding mallet, repeating the earlier example. The visible terminal comma is preserved rather than repaired to a period.

runs.text: E o de mais, ou outras couſas.

lines.note: Nado means and the rest or other things, the enumerative use. The scan separates E o; OCR Eo incorrectly joined the conjunction and article.
This separate Nado, alternatively nadoca and equated with Najoni, means why. The final S. marks written usage and is kept outside the italic translation.
Nagaame denotes prolonged spring rains. Two a letters distinguish the headword from Nagame later in the page; the scan supports Chuuas, correcting OCR Chauas.
Completes the defining duration of the spring rains. This short row belongs to Nagaame and does not qualify the following clothing entry.
Nagabacama refers to long hakama, rendered as long trousers. The voiced b in the compound is preserved rather than replaced by the independent form's h-row spelling.
Nagabanaxi is a lengthy conversation or talk. Portuguese pratica here denotes discourse, not merely repeated practice of an activity.
Nagabitçu names a long chest. The headword is abraded, but the surviving descending g, bi, and tçu support this reading; OCR Na, abicgu creates false segmentation and an implausible ending.

runs.text: O ladrar muito o cão como vyuan-

lines.note: Nagaboye denotes a dog's prolonged barking or howling. The Portuguese word vyuando is divided across the column boundary, not completed by the page's bottom catchword.
Do completes vyuando from column 1. Inu ga nagaboye wo suru illustrates a dog barking or howling for a long time; La- starts its Portuguese translation.

runs.text: drar o cão muito tempo como vyuando de noi-

lines.note: Completes ladrar and describes prolonged, howl-like barking at night. The scan includes y in vyuando, omitted by the OCR; noi- continues as noite below.
Te completes noite, night, in the preceding barking example. The small row closes Nagaboye before the next headword begins.
Nagacamoji is a long hairpiece or head of hair for women, as the Portuguese cabeleira indicates. The compound is preserved without replacing camoji with a modern explanatory term.
Nagadôriǔ denotes a long stay or prolonged sojourn. The circumflex over o and caron over u are separately visible and retained.
Nagagatana is a very long sword. The voiced g in the compound and the Portuguese loanword Catana are reproduced as printed.

runs.text: Hũa maneira de barretes que tem

lines.note: Nagagoyui names a kind of cap. The next row identifies its distinguishing two long points rather than its material or the wearer's rank.
Specifies the cap's two long points. This is the physical feature supplied by the dictionary, without reconstructing an exact cap design.
Nagaguſocu denotes long weapons, illustrated first by a lance. The remaining example continues on the following row.
Adds the halberd to the examples of long weapons. The short continuation belongs to Nagaguſocu, not to the adjective Nagai below.

runs.text: Couſa cõprida, ou que dura muito tẽpo.

lines.note: Nagai covers both spatial length and long duration. The tildes abbreviate nasal material in cõprida and tẽpo and remain unexpanded.
Nagaſa is the corresponding noun, length or duration. It is printed as its own indented physical row under Nagai, not as an independently defined entry.
Nagǒ is the contracted adverbial form associated with Nagai. Its caron is visible; the form is not replaced by modern nagaku.
Nagaiqi denotes a long life. The repeated form with its object particle begins the example completed by suru below.
Completes nagaiqi wo suru, living a long time. The Japanese example and Portuguese translation make clear that the length is temporal.
Nagame is gazing or extending one's view. The definition continues with a pleasing object and then supplies an example of looking at the surrounding scenery.
The gaze rests on something pleasant. Yomo no qe- begins the example concerning scenery in all directions, with qexiqi divided at the line break.
Completes yomo no qexiqi wo nagamuru, viewing the surrounding scenery for enjoyment. The printed Portuguese per is retained, not changed to the por later in the same line.
Completes looking in all directions. The translation corroborates yomo and closes the verbal entry before the noun Nagame follows.
The noun Nagame means a view or prospect. Its example begins with a view being different and continues with the evening on the next row.

runs.text: A viſta deſtatarde he differente das

lines.note: Yǔbe denotes the evening, not the OCR's yibe. The visible caron and the Portuguese tarde agree; das, not du, introduces comparison with other evenings, the tightly joined deſtatarde is retained rather than respaced from modern syntax.
Outras completes the comparison with other evenings or their views. It is the end of the example, not an omitted headword.
Nagameyari means casting one's gaze outward. The definition continues with distance, while the abbreviated principal parts remain exactly as printed.
The example looks far away toward the sky in that direction. Faruba- is the first part of farubaruto, retained at its physical division.
Completes the distant, honorific act of looking. The spaced nagame yari is kept; Taif. is the printed upright citation label, without expanding or respelling its title.

runs.text: Lib. 4. Lançando os olhos pera os ceos

lines.note: The citation specifies book 4, then translates casting one's eyes toward the skies. Lib. and the book number belong to the italic apparatus, unlike the preceding source label.
Completes the direction and distance of the gaze, toward that region far away. The printed ß in deßa is retained as a graphic feature.
Nagamochi names a long Japanese chest. Iapão is the Portuguese country name in the gloss, not a Japanese term to mark for whole-word typeface toggling.
Nagamonogatari denotes a lengthy tale or discourse, glossed like Nagabanaxi as long conversation. The entry is distinct even though the Portuguese wording repeats.
Naganaga is an adverb meaning at great length. Its definition continues with a temporal paraphrase and an example of a prolonged stay.
The temporal sense is for a long time. Naganaga tôriǔ begins an example of staying somewhere for an extended period, completed by suru below.
Completes the example of making a long stay. Detença is a sojourn here, not necessarily imprisonment or involuntary detention.
Naganagaxij describes something very long, either in extent or duration. Its ii-like final ij is retained as the dictionary's adjectival notation.
Completes the long-duration sense of Naganagaxij. The physical row remains separate despite containing only a short continuation.
This Nagaqiyo means long nights and carries the upright P. label for poetic usage. The label is moved outside the italic gloss without changing its wording.
The identically spelled expression here concerns a lasting world or eternal life. The dictionary distinguishes it from the preceding long-night entry by meaning.
Nagara first receives a concessive interpretation, although or even though. Fabacari begins the example of a deferential reservation continued below.
Fabacari nagara is rendered as although it may be discourtesy. The scan has deſcorteſia, with i before a, not OCR deſcorteſſa; the visible word and the noun meaning agree.
Adds a together sense, equated with the standalone Japanese synonym Tomoni. Futari na- begins the example meaning both people together; Tomoni is not embedded within a Portuguese sentence.
Completes Futari nagara and its translation, both together. Item introduces another construction on the next row rather than a new headword.
Introduces remaining just as one was. Qirumono to begins the coordinated clothing phrase in the example of entering water still dressed.
The person becomes immersed in water while still wearing clothing and an outer garment. The Portuguese begins Aßi; the OCR's extra t is absent from the visible type.

runs.text: como eſtaua veſtido cõ Dôbucu ſe ẽſopou nagoa.

lines.note: The translation confirms getting soaked in water while still dressed in Dôbucu. Its o has a circumflex, not the OCR grave; the embedded garment name is recorded for typeface review.
Nagaraye means continuing to live. The example starts Inochi, life, and supplies its object particle and verb on the next row.
Completes inochi wo nagarayuru, prolonging or sustaining one's life. Idem refers to the preceding living sense; the historical -yuru form is not modernized.
Nagare is the flowing of water or another liquid. The Portuguese adjective liquida is divided after li- at the visible line-end mark.
Completes liquida and illustrates tears flowing. Cor- begins the translation continued in the body of f347; the lower rerem is an anticipatory catchword, not an extra body row.
The catchword repeats the continuation of Cor- at the top of the next supplied page. Its italic type is distinguished from the draft's display classification.
